title: Energy realities derail COP31 | Wood Mackenzie
gist: Wood Mackenzie's Simon Flowers argues COP31 in Antalya became the first COP since 2009 to end without a core agreement because energy security, war-driven price shocks and assertive oil and gas exporters pushed climate down government priorities. Fossil fuels (80% of global energy demand) will stay critical for decades, competitiveness rather than diplomacy will drive the transition, and the collapse may ease approvals of new upstream projects in importers such as the UK.

themes.theme: COP31 Antalya collapse: no consensus on fossil fuel transition text

insights.claim: COP31, hosted by Türkiye with Australia as President of Negotiations, ended with no consensus and no final draft, making it the first COP since 2009 to conclude without a core agreement.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Multilateral climate policy is losing force as a driver of energy capital allocation, lowering policy risk for hydrocarbons.
insights.quote: the first COP since 2009 to conclude without a core agreement
insights.locator: Talks on the proposed Antalya Pact

insights.claim: The proposed Antalya Pact at COP31 included seemingly realistic targets of 35% electrification of final energy by 2035, just transition provisions, tripling climate finance and deploying carbon capture and storage, but talks broke down over text to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The sticking point was explicitly fossil fuel phase-out language, signalling that producer resistance, not technology targets, is the binding constraint on climate deals.
insights.quote: deep divisions around the text to “transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems” proved unbridgeable
insights.locator: Talks on the proposed Antalya Pact

themes.theme: Energy security displaces climate as government priority

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie argues that fragmentation of the rules-based international order, trade disputes and the wars in Ukraine and Iran have elevated energy security above climate change as many governments' primary focus, progressively weakening collective resolve on global warming this decade.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Policy support is shifting toward security of supply, favouring domestic production and diversified imports over pure decarbonisation spending.
insights.quote: have elevated energy security above climate change as many governments’ primary focus
insights.locator: The fragmentation of the rules-based international order

insights.claim: Fossil fuels still meet 80% of global energy demand and remain the backbone of the energy system in virtually all countries, eleven years after the Paris Agreement, with global energy demand rising faster than supply.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Demand growth outpacing supply underpins the case that hydrocarbon demand will persist despite renewables growth.
insights.quote: Fossil fuels remain the backbone of the energy system in virtually all countries, meeting 80% of global energy demand.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie judges that supply disruptions and spiralling oil and LNG prices triggered by the Iran war exposed the vulnerability of import-dependent countries but have not fundamentally changed the energy transition outlook.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Investors should not assume the Iran war price shock will structurally accelerate (or derail) the transition.
insights.quote: neither has fundamentally changed the outlook

themes.theme: Oil and gas exporters gain leverage; fossil fuels persist for decades

insights.claim: Resource-rich oil and gas exporters successfully kept any reference to phasing out fossil fuels out of the COP31 text because accelerating electrification, most likely in importing countries, threatens their economic future.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Producer states are actively and effectively defending long-term hydrocarbon demand in multilateral forums.
insights.quote: Fossil fuel producers seized their opportunity in Antalya.
insights.locator: Fossil fuel producers seized their opportunity

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's Energy Transition Outlook forecasts that fossil fuels will continue to play a critical part in energy security for decades to come, regardless of COP phase-out language.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Supports a long-duration view on oil and gas assets and infrastructure.
insights.quote: fossil fuels will continue to play a critical part in energy security for decades to come
insights.locator: Fossil fuel producers seized their opportunity

themes.theme: Competitiveness, not diplomacy, drives the energy mix

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie holds that competitiveness ultimately determines the energy mix: renewables are competitive in most power markets and will keep growing alongside batteries and electric vehicles, while oil and gas at current elevated prices cannot compete.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Low-carbon growth is economically self-sustaining even without COP agreements, supporting renewables, storage and EV supply chains.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie expects currently elevated oil and gas prices could soon fall sharply.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: A sharp hydrocarbon price decline would hit producer earnings and restore fossil fuel competitiveness versus alternatives.
insights.quote: our expectation is that prices could soon fall – and sharply

insights.claim: With power demand rising quickly due to data centres, electric vehicles and advanced manufacturing, some countries may pragmatically soften their anti-fossil fuel stance and let the current energy mix persist.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: AI/data-centre-driven power demand growth is a tailwind for gas-fired generation and slows coal and gas retirements.
insights.quote: some countries may take a pragmatic view, soften their anti-fossil fuels stance and allow the current energy mix to persist

themes.theme: Second-order benefit for importers: new upstream approvals in Europe and the UK

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie argues that some oil and gas importers, including Europe, may benefit from COP31 omitting fossil fuel phase-out text, because Europe remains a major oil and gas importer despite leading on climate policy.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Counterintuitively, a weaker climate deal may improve European energy security options and upstream investment prospects.
insights.quote: some oil and gas importers – Europe included – may actually benefit from the omission of the text on fossil fuels
insights.locator: Third, some oil and gas importers

insights.claim: The failure of the COP31 talks in Antalya may smooth the path for European governments such as the UK, currently in a quandary over approving new domestic oil and gas investment, to greenlight new upstream projects.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Raises the probability of new North Sea-style upstream approvals, positive for domestic E&Ps and oilfield services.
insights.quote: The failure of talks in Antalya may smooth the path for these governments to greenlight new upstream projects.
insights.locator: While Europe is at the vanguard

themes.theme: Global climate leadership vacuum: US absence and China's choice

insights.claim: The US absence from both COP30 and COP31 undermined consensus, and a US return to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, signalled by the Democratic party, realistically requires a 2028 presidential win even with Democratic majorities in both chambers of Congress after the midterms.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
entities: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change
insights.so_what: US federal climate re-engagement is at least two years away, extending the current policy backdrop for US oil and gas.
insights.quote: it will take victory in the 2028 presidential election for this to become a realistic prospect
insights.locator: Fourth, there is a global leadership vacuum

insights.claim: With affordability top of the US political agenda, curtailing oil and gas investment does not look like a vote winner, according to Wood Mackenzie.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Even a Democratic-led US is unlikely to aggressively restrict oil and gas investment.
insights.quote: With affordability top of the political agenda, curtailing investment in oil and gas doesn’t look a vote winner.
insights.locator: Fourth, there is a global leadership vacuum

insights.claim: China has chosen not to take up an available global climate leadership role, likely because its dominance in manufacturing and exporting low-carbon technologies and in critical minerals for the transition is a sufficient prize.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: China's transition strategy is commercial and industrial rather than diplomatic, reinforcing its grip on clean-tech and minerals supply chains.
insights.quote: Its position as the global pacesetter in manufacturing and exporting low-carbon technologies and dominance of critical minerals for the transition may be proving a sufficient prize.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie sees belief in future COPs' ability to deliver global climate action as wafer-thin, meaning countries will increasingly determine their own energy futures unilaterally amid a broader failure of global institutions on climate, conflict and trade.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Energy policy fragmentation means country-by-country policy analysis matters more than global climate targets for investment decisions.
insights.quote: Belief in the ability of future COPs to deliver global action is now wafer-thin
insights.locator: Belief in the ability of future
